value.overview: The Middle American Leaftosser, also called the Tawny-throated Leaftosser, is a secretive forest bird of the ovenbird family. It spends much of its time on the ground, using its bill to toss aside dead leaves while searching for small invertebrates. Its mostly brown plumage provides excellent camouflage, while the warm tawny throat and chest are useful identification features. The species is usually encountered alone or in pairs in humid tropical forest.
value.classification: The Middle American Leaftosser belongs to the family Furnariidae, the ovenbirds and woodcreepers, and the subfamily Sclerurinae. Its scientific name is Sclerurus mexicanus.
value.identification: This small, compact leaftosser is about 15–17 cm long. Adults are mainly dark brown above and below, with a distinctive tawny to rufous throat and upper breast. The back and wings are plain, the rump may appear somewhat warmer chestnut, and the tail is short and dark. It has a fairly long, pointed bill and strong legs suited to ground foraging. Its low posture, secretive behavior, and habit of flipping leaves help separate it from similar forest understory birds.
value.rangeHabitat: The species occurs from southern Mexico through much of Central America to western Panama. In Costa Rica it is a resident of humid forested areas, especially foothills, montane and premontane forest, and forested highlands; the Costa Rican population is associated with the form Sclerurus mexicanus pullus. It generally favors shaded, leaf-littered forest floors and can occur from lowlands into the highlands, commonly at roughly 700–2,200 meters, depending on locality. It is most likely in mature, continuous forest.
value.migrationStatus: Resident in Costa Rica and across its range; it does not undertake regular long-distance migration. Local movements may occur in response to food, weather, or habitat conditions.
value.breeding: Breeding information is best documented in Costa Rica, where nesting occurs mainly from December through April. Pairs are territorial and apparently monogamous. The nest is placed in a short burrow excavated in an earth bank or similar protected site, sometimes using a natural cavity or abandoned opening. It is lined with small sticks and leaves. The clutch typically contains two unmarked white eggs. Adults share territorial defense and care for the young, although many details of parental behavior remain poorly known.
value.dietFeeding: The Middle American Leaftosser feeds mainly on small invertebrates, including insects, spiders, beetles, ants, roaches, larvae, and other arthropods. It forages primarily on the forest floor, hopping through damp leaf litter and turning leaves with its bill. It also probes rotting wood, loose soil, and decomposing vegetation. Individuals usually forage alone or in pairs, relying on stealth rather than conspicuous movement.
value.behavior: This is a quiet, elusive bird that spends much of its time in dense understory or on the ground. It commonly moves by short hops while tossing leaves aside, and it may freeze or slip into cover when approached. Pairs defend territories and may remain in the same forest area throughout the year. Its song consists of a descending series of plaintive, drawn-out notes, while alarm calls are sharper and more abrupt. It is more often heard than seen.

conservation.populationTrend: A precise global population estimate and reliably quantified trend are not available.
